[[:db/retract 17592186134055 :question/answer-fields 17592186130486] {:db/id 17592186133871 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7f21c5fc-f92d-5b81-95e0-bb89748670fa" "question-e1da803c-87de-5156-b3a7-d636001e9616" "question-0be806ce-1a6b-5ee1-964b-e362c3c8599e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133687 :question/problem "![](images/d2/d28edbbb8741260e5087e4ecc1424d03208354580d8aff6e2baeae01ba8d2c97.svg)
Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^3$ is defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = 3x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp \mathbf{v}_2$ with respect to the given inner product

II. $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp \mathbf{v}_3$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133870 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c3a213f9-9ffe-56d7-a8aa-efb68c3978ef"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133686 :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
p_1(t)=t+1, \qquad
p_2(t)=t, \qquad
p_3(t)=t-1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathbb{R}_1[t]$ of polynomials of degree $1$ or less in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
\langle p(t),q(t) \rangle =p(-1)q(-1)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. $p_2(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133688 :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
f_1(t)=1, \qquad
f_2(t)=t, \qquad
f_3(t)=2t+1
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
\langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. $f_2(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7f21c5fc-f92d-5b81-95e0-bb89748670fa" :question/id #uuid "7f21c5fc-f92d-5b81-95e0-bb89748670fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-140497" :question/problem "$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩=5{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${v}_{2}⊥̸{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =5(1)(-1)+(1)(7)+2(1)(-1) \\  & =-5+7-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =5(-1)(2)+(7)(0)+2(-1)(-5) \\  & =-10+0+10 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =5(1)(2)+(1)(0)+2(1)(-5) \\  & =10+0-10 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be0c4698-714b-5480-a266-83cfdfc1738d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-be0c4698-714b-5480-a266-83cfdfc1738d" :answer-field/id #uuid "be0c4698-714b-5480-a266-83cfdfc1738d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c2ae49b3-2b1a-5769-a32d-2fa88e84403a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f74c6690-ce28-580c-9560-4db51296ad3f" "answer-c2ae49b3-2b1a-5769-a32d-2fa88e84403a" "answer-db41afa9-b02c-5090-94ff-3130841b1e75" "answer-5292133c-58a4-54a4-a601-35a908997fea" "answer-821647ea-8e8f-5c03-ba00-206492b1131a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f74c6690-ce28-580c-9560-4db51296ad3f" :answer/id #uuid "f74c6690-ce28-580c-9560-4db51296ad3f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c2ae49b3-2b1a-5769-a32d-2fa88e84403a" :answer/id #uuid "c2ae49b3-2b1a-5769-a32d-2fa88e84403a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db41afa9-b02c-5090-94ff-3130841b1e75" :answer/id #uuid "db41afa9-b02c-5090-94ff-3130841b1e75" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5292133c-58a4-54a4-a601-35a908997fea" :answer/id #uuid "5292133c-58a4-54a4-a601-35a908997fea" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-821647ea-8e8f-5c03-ba00-206492b1131a" :answer/id #uuid "821647ea-8e8f-5c03-ba00-206492b1131a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134560 :question/problem "$$

{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩=2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+3{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥̸{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =2(2)(1)+3(-1)(1)+(1)(-1) \\  & =4-3-1 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =2(1)(0)+3(1)(1)+(-1)(3) \\  & =0+3-3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =2(2)(0)+3(-1)(1)+(1)(3) \\  & =0-3+3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-715169d2-6248-5c13-8e14-43b51e80908b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-715169d2-6248-5c13-8e14-43b51e80908b" :answer-field/id #uuid "715169d2-6248-5c13-8e14-43b51e80908b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-518b0bf4-0290-5996-ba11-0aede8ea3071" :answer-field/choices ["answer-680ba569-6fa1-5174-a88b-6fec3325f8fd" "answer-eeedd419-cbf7-5753-9977-4da6fe0c9b81" "answer-518b0bf4-0290-5996-ba11-0aede8ea3071" "answer-c8647e45-9ab4-56a3-93bb-8a30b093366b" "answer-27c15540-3c41-5ca2-a7d9-dc8baf6f1008"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-680ba569-6fa1-5174-a88b-6fec3325f8fd" :answer/id #uuid "680ba569-6fa1-5174-a88b-6fec3325f8fd" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eeedd419-cbf7-5753-9977-4da6fe0c9b81" :answer/id #uuid "eeedd419-cbf7-5753-9977-4da6fe0c9b81" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-518b0bf4-0290-5996-ba11-0aede8ea3071" :answer/id #uuid "518b0bf4-0290-5996-ba11-0aede8ea3071" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c8647e45-9ab4-56a3-93bb-8a30b093366b" :answer/id #uuid "c8647e45-9ab4-56a3-93bb-8a30b093366b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-27c15540-3c41-5ca2-a7d9-dc8baf6f1008" :answer/id #uuid "27c15540-3c41-5ca2-a7d9-dc8baf6f1008" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134568 :question/problem "$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+4{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(4)(-8)+(-2)(4)+4(2)(5) \\  & =-32-8+40 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(4)(1)+(-2)(2)+4(2)(0) \\  & =4-4+0 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(-8)(1)+(4)(2)+4(5)(0) \\  & =-8+8+0 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133446 :answer-field/correct 17592186133450 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-0be806ce-1a6b-5ee1-964b-e362c3c8599e" :question/id #uuid "0be806ce-1a6b-5ee1-964b-e362c3c8599e" :question/math-academy-id "q-140495" :question/problem "$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩=2{x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+3{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =2(1)(3)+2(0)(1)+3(2)(-1) \\  & =6+0-6 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true since 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =2(1)(-9)+2(0)(-2)+3(2)(3) \\  & =-18+0+18 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}.$ Computing the inner product, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =2(3)(-9)+2(1)(-2)+3(-1)(3) \\  & =-54-4-9 \\  & =-67\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥̸{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
Since ${v}_{2}⊥̸{v}_{3},$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-68a628e9-2427-55d0-991e-370a53971bc4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-68a628e9-2427-55d0-991e-370a53971bc4" :answer-field/id #uuid "68a628e9-2427-55d0-991e-370a53971bc4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2d39f349-998b-59ff-bf35-dc110bf6bf2e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2d39f349-998b-59ff-bf35-dc110bf6bf2e" "answer-a6621b58-77e4-59d2-b684-96f69b011cd8" "answer-fb73d8fe-92a2-5daf-a18a-f4c0dec77755" "answer-dbb7dce8-d733-517f-ba5b-5223c54118a3" "answer-8f2d2cfb-c614-5b27-bc96-e076f598725f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2d39f349-998b-59ff-bf35-dc110bf6bf2e" :answer/id #uuid "2d39f349-998b-59ff-bf35-dc110bf6bf2e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a6621b58-77e4-59d2-b684-96f69b011cd8" :answer/id #uuid "a6621b58-77e4-59d2-b684-96f69b011cd8" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fb73d8fe-92a2-5daf-a18a-f4c0dec77755" :answer/id #uuid "fb73d8fe-92a2-5daf-a18a-f4c0dec77755" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dbb7dce8-d733-517f-ba5b-5223c54118a3" :answer/id #uuid "dbb7dce8-d733-517f-ba5b-5223c54118a3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8f2d2cfb-c614-5b27-bc96-e076f598725f" :answer/id #uuid "8f2d2cfb-c614-5b27-bc96-e076f598725f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134055 :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(-1)q(-1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134559 :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

III. $S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,t-1⟩ \\  & =(t){|}_{0}\cdot (t-1){|}_{0}+(t){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =0\cdot (0-1)+1\cdot (1-1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,2t-2⟩ \\  & =(t){|}_{0}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{0}+(t){|}_{1}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{1} \\  & =0\cdot (2(0)-2)+1\cdot (2(1)-2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-1,2t-2⟩ \\  & =(t-1){|}_{0}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{0}+(t-1){|}_{1}\cdot (2t-2){|}_{1} \\  & =(0-1)\cdot (2(0)-2)+(1-1)\cdot (2(1)-2) \\  & =2\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨3t,{t}^{2}-1⟩ \\  & =(3t){|}_{-1}\cdot ({t}^{2}-1){|}_{-1}+(3t){|}_{0}\cdot ({t}^{2}-1){|}_{0}+(3t){|}_{1}\cdot ({t}^{2}-1){|}_{1} \\  & =(3(-1))\cdot ((-1)^{2}-1)+(3(0))\cdot ({0}^{2}-1)+(3(1))\cdot ({1}^{2}-1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* an orthogonal set.

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135104 :tutorial/content "Let's consider an inner product space $V$ equipped with the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$ 
A set of vectors 

$$
{U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}
$$

is called an **orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product** if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the set

![](images/69/69571997d87ed3f40ee7e9b0742075fbd5ee107892f6a9b4198f75f3f5a9fce3.svg)

and the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 + 3x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${V}$ as $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \},$ we can check that ${V}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each inner product:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(2)+3(1)(2)+2(1)(-4)=2+6-8=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(-3)+3(1)(1)+2(1)(0)=-3+3+0=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(2)(-3)+3(2)(1)+2(-4)(0)=-6+6+0=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${V}$ is an orthogonal set." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133991 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Whether a Set of Polynomials is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product"}] :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
p_1(t)=t+1, \qquad
p_2(t)=t, \qquad
p_3(t)=t-1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathbb{R}_1[t]$ of polynomials of degree $1$ or less in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
\langle p(t),q(t) \rangle =p(-1)q(-1)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

- $p_2(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

- $S=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t+1,t-1⟩ \\  & =(t+1){|}_{-1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{-1}+(t+1){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =(-1+1)\cdot (-1-1)+(1+1)\cdot (1-1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,t-1⟩ \\  & =(t){|}_{-1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{-1}+(t){|}_{1}\cdot (t-1){|}_{1} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1-1)+(1)\cdot (1-1) \\  & =2\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $p_2(t) \not\perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since $p_2(t) \not\perp p_3(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186134055 :question/id #uuid "97d43a34-aeb6-5e6a-8281-47dcdcd73020" :question/math-academy-id "q-100128" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=t+1,\,{p}_{3}(t)=2t+1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(-1)q(-1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t,t+1⟩ \\  & =(2t){|}_{0}\cdot (t+1){|}_{0}+(2t){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1} \\  & =2(0)\cdot (0+1)+2(-1)\cdot ((-1)+1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t,2t+1⟩ \\  & =(2t){|}_{0}\cdot (2t+1){|}_{0}+(2t){|}_{-1}\cdot (2t+1){|}_{-1} \\  & =2(0)\cdot (2(0)+1)+2(-1)\cdot (2(-1)+1) \\  & =2\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t-1,\,{p}_{2}(t)=3t,\,{p}_{3}(t)=1-t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t-1,3t⟩ \\  & =(2t-1){|}_{0}\cdot (3t){|}_{0}+(2t-1){|}_{1}\cdot (3t){|}_{1} \\  & =(2(0)-1)\cdot (3(0))+(2(1)-1)\cdot (3(1)) \\  & =3\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨3t,1-t⟩ \\  & =(3t){|}_{0}\cdot (1-t){|}_{0}+(3t){|}_{1}\cdot (1-t){|}_{1} \\  & =(3(0))\cdot (1-0)+(3(1))\cdot (1-1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186237780 :question/id #uuid "e68e3d26-aa65-5eb7-b898-7c00e9b7271e" :question/math-academy-id "q-100091" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133870 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c2bcfcb6-8f8b-5aa9-8346-05db880fa5bb" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether a Set of Polynomials is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4e1d6561-f56d-53c0-9b71-11bc0f759a6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186236317} {:answer/id #uuid "6814b5e7-1bc3-51d5-942c-c2e1d619b1c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186236476} {:answer/id #uuid "bc9a653b-e737-5dcb-9b56-f1a2267ae748" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186237022} {:answer/id #uuid "d4400354-4d53-5b51-b879-c0baabaca818" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements is true" :db/id 17592186237159} {:answer/id #uuid "f98acd17-31db-5102-8faf-75afbedcdd5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186237392}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f98acd17-31db-5102-8faf-75afbedcdd5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186237392} :answer-field/id #uuid "56faa6f3-ee6e-5488-a8ad-10874ae44edb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186237555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=t-1,\,{p}_{2}(t)=2,\,{p}_{3}(t)=t+1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-1,t+1⟩ \\  & =(t-1){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1}+(t-1){|}_{1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{1} \\  & =(-1-1)\cdot ((-1)+1)+(1-1)\cdot (1+1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2,t+1⟩ \\  & =(2){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1}+(2){|}_{1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{1} \\  & =(2)\cdot ((-1)+1)+(2)\cdot (1+1) \\  & =4\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${p}_{2}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

$$

:question/math-academy-id "e-8714" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186133872 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "382a6db7-2708-5711-885e-6f3f3037e8df" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product"}] :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
f_1(t)=1, \qquad
f_2(t)=t, \qquad
f_3(t)=2t+1
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
\langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

- $f_2(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

- $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨1,2t+1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}+t){|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & ={1}^{2}+1-((-1)^{2}+(-1)) \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,2t+1⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2{t}^{2}+t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2(1)^{3}}{3}+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-(\frac{2(-1)^{3}}{3}+\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $f_2(t) \not\perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186050929} {:db/id 17592186134561 :question/id #uuid "2a5307a8-8a58-5d9f-8aa3-c19ff22a65ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-98524" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133872 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "382a6db7-2708-5711-885e-6f3f3037e8df" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "257d7e25-c8e7-57e6-a4d4-aa21b511e781" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186360997} {:answer/id #uuid "4dfb964b-a6c1-501f-ab62-a62f50e19d4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186361176} {:answer/id #uuid "98da24fa-2af2-502b-9b77-30f454b71363" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186361518} {:answer/id #uuid "dea06f8a-28dd-5522-ac61-19c8d59aeb48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/id 17592186361830} {:answer/id #uuid "f44ba2cc-b923-5dd4-8a36-949b6970ee6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186361929}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "dea06f8a-28dd-5522-ac61-19c8d59aeb48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/id 17592186361830} :answer-field/id #uuid "1900c13c-3fc3-5304-bb7b-280cc216d669" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186362003}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{3}(t)=t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi ]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi ]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ))-\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,t⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t){|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =0+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186134569 :question/id #uuid "a07c5a93-5161-56bc-aa10-7d11733928e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-99808"} {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={e}^{t},\,{f}_{3}(t)={e}^{-t}
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-{e}^{t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(e+{e}^{-1})-(e-{e}^{-1}) \\  & =2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t,{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=-{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-1}^{1}-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1}+{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-{e}^{-t}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-{e}^{-1}-e)-({e}^{-1}-e) \\  & =-2{e}^{-1}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true.""} {:db/id 17592186272132 :question/id #uuid "1e4b04d4-e7d3-5042-809a-2a3512a7a902" :question/math-academy-id "q-140556" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133872 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "382a6db7-2708-5711-885e-6f3f3037e8df" :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0562db51-66a7-5a18-a492-af715264f543" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186269315} {:answer/id #uuid "71005342-d55f-5332-b578-95e6f906faab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186270273} {:answer/id #uuid "a0c3fac8-64b6-560e-a9cd-252aed9b1291" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186270694} {:answer/id #uuid "e3d033de-73ce-5f72-b75d-36907f8d890e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186271275} {:answer/id #uuid "f223e07f-474f-53ea-9772-c00afbe6a869" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186271394}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "a0c3fac8-64b6-560e-a9cd-252aed9b1291" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186270694} :answer-field/id #uuid "7165e98a-3520-5bd3-93ee-a5107bf92b82" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186271710}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=2(t-1),\,{f}_{2}(t)={e}^{t},\,{f}_{3}(t)={e}^{(t-1)^{2}}
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,2]$ of continuous functions over $[0,2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2(t-1),{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2(t-1)({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2(t-1) & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=2, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}2(t-1){e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{2}-{\int }_{0}^{2}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2(t-1){e}^{t}){|}_{0}^{2}-{\int }_{0}^{2}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2{e}^{2}-(-2))-2{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2}+2-(2{e}^{2}-2) \\  & =4\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2(t-1),{e}^{(t-1)^{2}}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2(t-1){e}^{(t-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={e}^{(t-1)^{2}}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =e-e \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{2},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2t)}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)}{4}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )}{4})-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-5t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+5t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-4t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4t)}{4}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)}{6}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )}{4}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )}{6})-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{4}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t),$ ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ and ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186362394 :question/id #uuid "8889f645-9334-518f-83dc-7064dd4f1d1d" :question/math-academy-id "q-99848"} {:db/id 17592186362397 17592186382669}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨t,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )}{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )}{2})+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{4}{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =0+(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{4}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )}{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{u}^{′}v\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}+{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(-(-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})))+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =0+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =1-(-1) \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186382675 :question/id #uuid "866dfd7d-0156-5915-b7a2-48bb304694df" :question/math-academy-id "q-99949"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id [{:db/id 17592186134813 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135104 :tutorial/content "Let's consider an inner product space $V$ equipped with the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$ 
A set of vectors 

$$
{U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}
$$

is called an **orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product** if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the set

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

and the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 + 3x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${V}$ as $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \},$ we can check that ${V}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each inner product:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(2)+3(1)(2)+2(1)(-4)=2+6-8=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(-3)+3(1)(1)+2(1)(0)=-3+3+0=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(2)(-3)+3(2)(1)+2(-4)(0)=-6+6+0=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${V}$ is an orthogonal set." :tutorial/id #uuid "f5f69210-8732-5a94-b16b-b7de520cfc66" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5149 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186134813 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135104 :tutorial/content "Let's consider an inner product space $V$ equipped with the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$ 
A set of vectors 

$$
{U}=\{ \mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}
$$

is called an **orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product** if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal.

For example, let's consider the set

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

and the inner product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 + 3x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.
$$

If we denote the vectors in our set ${V}$ as $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \},$ we can check that ${V}$ is orthogonal by showing that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩=0 \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute each inner product:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(2)+3(1)(2)+2(1)(-4)=2+6-8=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(-3)+3(1)(1)+2(1)(0)=-3+3+0=0 & ✓ \\ ⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(2)(-3)+3(2)(1)+2(-4)(0)=-6+6+0=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So indeed, ${V}$ is an orthogonal set." :tutorial/id #uuid "f5f69210-8732-5a94-b16b-b7de520cfc66" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5149 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "520866ac-288a-5e25-aa54-cc9335b03e13" :step/math-academy-id 32389 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134815}} {:db/id 17592186135104 :tutorial/content "Let's consider an inner product space $V$ equipped with the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$

for the Physical Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in
